metadata.title: Bounds on the exceptional set in the $abc$ conjecture

nodes.statement: {} For $\lambda>0$ define $N_\lambda(X)$ as the number of triples $(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^3$ with $a+b=c$, $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and $\rad(abc) < c^{\lambda}$.
nodes.label: def:Nlambda

nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon>0$, we have \begin{equation} \#\left\{n\leqslant x : \rad(n)\leqslant x^\lambda\right\} \ll_\varepsilon x^{\lambda+\varepsilon}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:deBruijnRadical

nodes.statement: It suffices to show that for any integer $k\geqslant 2$ we have \begin{align} |\{n\leqslant X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}|\ll X^{O(1/\log \log X)}. \end{align} To prove \eqref{eq1}, write $k=p_1\cdots p_r$ as distinct primes $p_1<\cdots <p_r$. Then $\rad(n)=k$ implies that $n=p_1^{m_1}\cdots p_{r}^{m_r}$ for some integers $m_1,\ldots, m_r\geqslant 1$. Therefore, the number of $n\leqslant X$ in question is \begin{align*} |\{n\leqslant X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}| &\leqslant \sum_{m_1,\ldots, m_r\geqslant 1}\1_{\sum_{j\leqslant r}m_j(\log p_j)\leqslant \log X}\\ &\leqslant \sum_{m_1,\ldots, m_r\geqslant 1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^r}\1_{\sum_{j\leqslant r}t_j(\log p_j)\leqslant \log X}\1_{t_j\in (m_j-1,m_j]\, \forall j\leqslant r} \textnormal{d} t_1\cdots \textnormal{d} t_r\\ &=\textnormal{vol}\Big(\big\{(t_1,\ldots, t_r)\in \mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}^r:\,\, t_1(\log p_1)+\cdots +t_r(\log p_r)\leqslant \log X\big\}\Big)\\ &=(\log X)^re^{O(r)}r^{-r}\prod_{j=1}^r \frac{1}{\log p_j} \end{align*} by calculating the volume of a simplex. Moreover, we have \begin{align*} \prod_{j=1}^r \log p_j\geqslant \prod_{j=2}^{r+1}\log j=\exp\left(\sum_{j=2}^{r+1}\log \log j\right)\gg (\log r)^{r}e^{-O(r)}. \end{align*} Hence for some $C_0>1$ \begin{align*} |\{n\leqslant X:\,\, \rad(n)=k\}| \ll \left(\frac{C_0\log X}{r\log r}\right)^r\ll \exp\Big(O\Big(\frac{\log X}{\log\log X}\Big)\Big), \end{align*} since $r=\omega(k)\leqslant (1+o(1))(\log X)/(\log \log X)$ by the prime number theorem.
Let $\lambda>0$. Then $N_\lambda(X)=O_\varepsilon( X^{2\lambda/3+\varepsilon})$, for any $\varepsilon>0$.
nodes.label: prop:ABCTrivialBound

nodes.statement: Any triple $(a,b,c)$ counted by $N_\lambda(X)$ must satisfy $\rad(abc)< X^{\lambda}$, and so we must have $\min\{\rad(a)\rad(b),\rad(b)\rad(c),\rad(c)\rad(a)\}< X^{2\lambda/3}$, since $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime. An application of~\ref{lem:deBruijnRadical} now leads to the following ``trivial bound''.
Let $\lambda\in (0, 1.001)$ be fixed. Then $N_\lambda(X)=O( X^{33/50})$.
nodes.label: thm:ABCExceptionalBound

nodes.statement: For $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$, define $S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$ as the number of $(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^3$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ such that \[ a,b,c\in [1,X], \quad a+b=c, \quad \rad(a)\leqslant X^\alpha, \quad \rad(b)\leqslant X^\beta, \quad \rad(c)\leqslant X^\gamma. \]
nodes.label: def:Sabc

nodes.statement: \begin{equation} S_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_\varepsilon X^{\min\{\alpha+\beta , \alpha+\gamma , \beta+\gamma\}+\varepsilon}, \end{equation} for any $\varepsilon>0$.
nodes.label: lem:TrivialBdforS

nodes.statement: Let $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$ to be the number of $(a,b,c)\in \mathbb{N}^3$ with $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and \begin{align*} c\in [X/2,X],\quad a+b=c,\quad \rad(a)\sim X^{\alpha},\quad \rad(b)\sim X^{\beta},\quad \rad(c)\sim X^{\gamma}. \end{align*}
nodes.label: def:Sstar

nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} N_\lambda(X)\ll (\log X)^4 \max_{\substack{ \alpha,\beta,\gamma>0\\ \alpha+\beta+\gamma\leqslant \lambda}} S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X). \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:NlambdatoSstar

nodes.statement: There exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that for all $\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ and $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d}$. we have \begin{align} B_d({\bf c, X,Y,Z}) \ll X^{0.66-\varepsilon}. \end{align}
nodes.label: thm:BdExceptionalBound

nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ and $\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}\in \mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d}$. we have \begin{equation} B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}) := \#\left\{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z})\in \mathbb{N}^{3d}\;:\; \begin{array}{l} x_i\sim X_i,\,y_i\sim Y_i,\,z_i\sim Z_i \\ c_1\prod_{j\leqslant d}x_j^j+c_2\prod_{j\leqslant d}y_j^j=c_3\prod_{j\leqslant d}z_j^j\\ \gcd(c_1\prod_{j\leqslant d}x_j,c_2\prod_{j\leqslant d}y_j , c_3\prod_{j\leqslant d}z_j)=1 \end{array} \right\}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: def:BdDiophantineCount

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon\in (0,1/2)$, and let $2\leqslant n\leqslant X$ be an integer. Then there exists a factorisation \begin{align*} n=c\prod_{j\leqslant \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}}x_j^{j}, \end{align*} for positive integers $x_j,c$ such that $c\leqslant X^{\varepsilon/2}$, the $x_j$ are pairwise coprime, and \begin{align*} X^{-\varepsilon}\prod_{j\leqslant \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}}x_j \leqslant \rad(n) \leqslant X^{\varepsilon}\prod_{j\leqslant \frac{5}{2}\varepsilon^{-2}}x_j. \end{align*}
nodes.label: lem:DiophantineFactor

Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in (0,1]$ be fixed and let $X\geqslant 2$. For any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an integer $d=d(\varepsilon)\geqslant 1$ such that the following holds. There exist $X_1,\ldots, X_d,Y_1,\ldots, Y_d, Z_1,\ldots, Z_d\geqslant 1$ satisfying \begin{align} X^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^{d}X_j\leqslant 2 X^{\alpha+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\beta-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^{d}Y_j\leqslant 2 X^{\beta+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\gamma-\varepsilon}\ll_{\varepsilon}\prod_{j=1}^{d}Z_j\leqslant 2 X^{\gamma+\varepsilon} \end{align} and \begin{align} \prod_{j=1}^d X_j^j \leqslant X, \quad \prod_{j=1}^d Y_j^j\leqslant X,\quad X^{1-\varepsilon^2}\ll_{\varepsilon} \prod_{j=1}^d Z_j^j\leqslant X \end{align} and pairwise coprime integers $1\leqslant c_1,c_2,c_3\leqslant X^{\varepsilon}$, such that \begin{align*} S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X) \ll_{\varepsilon} X^{\varepsilon}B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}). \end{align*}
nodes.label: prop:DiophantineReduction

nodes.statement: We may assume that $X$ is large enough in terms of $\varepsilon$, since otherwise the claim is trivial. Let $(a,b,c)$ be a triple counted by $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:DiophantineFactor} (with $\varepsilon^2/2$ in place of $\varepsilon$) to each of $a,b,c$ to obtain factorisations of the form \begin{align*} a=c_1\prod_{j\leqslant d}x_j^j,\quad b=c_2\prod_{j\leqslant d}y_j^j,\quad c=c_3\prod_{j\leqslant d}z_j^j, \end{align*} where $d=\lfloor 10\varepsilon^{-4}\rfloor$ and $1\leqslant c_1,c_2,c_3\leqslant X^{\varepsilon^2/4}$. Since $(a,b,c)$ is counted by $S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)$, we have $\gcd(a,b,c)=1$ and $a+b=c$, so $a,b,c$ are pairwise coprime. Hence, all the $3d+3$ numbers $x_i,y_i,z_i,c_1,c_2,c_3$ are pairwise coprime. Note also that by the properties of the factorisation given by Lemma~\ref{lem:DiophantineFactor}, we have \begin{align*} &X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leqslant d}x_j\leqslant \rad(a)\leqslant X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leqslant d}x_j,\quad X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leqslant d}y_j\leqslant \rad(b)\leqslant X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leqslant d}y_j,\\ &X^{-\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leqslant d}z_j\leqslant \rad(c)\leqslant X^{\varepsilon/2}\prod_{j\leqslant d}z_j. \end{align*} Since $\rad(a)\sim X^{\alpha},\rad(b)\sim X^{\beta},\rad(c)\sim X^{\gamma}$ for all triples under consideration, this implies \begin{align*} X^{\alpha-\varepsilon}\leqslant \prod_{j\leqslant d}x_j\leqslant X^{\alpha+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\beta-\varepsilon}\leqslant \prod_{j\leqslant d}y_j\leqslant X^{\beta+\varepsilon},\quad X^{\gamma-\varepsilon}\leqslant \prod_{j\leqslant d}z_j\leqslant X^{\gamma+\varepsilon}. \end{align*} By dyadic decomposition, we can now find some $X_i, Y_i,Z_i$ such that~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_1} and~\eqref{eq:xiyizi_2} hold, and such that \[ S^*_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(X)\ll_{\varepsilon} (\log X)^{3d} \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{c}\in \mathbb{N}^3\\ c_1,c_2,c_3 \leqslant X^{\varepsilon/4}}}B_d(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{Z}). \] Now the claim follows from the pigeonhole principle.

Let $d\geqslant 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ be fixed, and let \[ X_1,\ldots, X_d, Y_1,\ldots, Y_d,Z_1,\ldots, Z_d\geqslant 1. \] Let $\mathbf{c}\in (c_1,c_2,c_3)\in \mathbb{Z}^3$ have non-zero and pairwise coprime coordinates. Let $\gcd(a_1,a_2,a_3)=1$. Then for $X_1,X_2,X_3>1$, we have \begin{align*} \#\left((x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb{Z}^3 \;:\; \gcd(x_1,x_2,x_3)=1,\, |x_i| \leqslant X_i ,\, a_1x_1+a_2x_2+a_3x_3=0\right) \ll \ 1 \ + \ & \frac{X_1X_2X_3}{\max_i\{|a_i|X_i\}}. \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:HeathBrownGeometry

nodes.statement: Let $r\geqslant 1$ and let $g\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ be a polynomial which has at least one root of multiplicity $1$. Then the polynomial $g(x)-y^r$ is absolutely irreducible.
nodes.label: lem:EisensteinCrit

nodes.statement: We may assume a factorisation $g(x)=l_1(x)^{e_1}\dots l_t(x)^{e_t}$, with pairwise non-proportional linear polynomials $l_1,\dots,l_t\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ and exponents $e_1,\dots,e_t\in \mathbb{N}$ such that $e_1=1$. But ${\mathbb{C}}[x]$ is a unique factorisation domain and so we can apply Eisenstein's criterion with the prime $l_1$ in order to deduce that $g(x)-y^r$ is irreducible over $ {\mathbb{C}}[y]$. It then follows that $g(x)-y^r$ is irreducible over $ \mathbb{C}$, as claimed in the lemma.

Let $f(x)$ be a $C^\infty$ function on a closed subinterval of $[0,N]$, and suppose that$F (x, f ) = 0$, where $F(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}[x, y]$ is absolutely irreducible of degree $d \geqslant 2$. Suppose that $|f'(x)| \leqslant 1$. Then \begin{align*} \#\{(x,f(x))\in \{1,\ldots,N\}^2 \} \ll_d (\log N)^{O(N)} N^{1/d} \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:BombieriPilaforDet

nodes.statement: Let $F\in \mathbb{Z}[x_1 ,\ldots, x_n]$ be an absolutely irreducible polynomial of degree $d$, and let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $B_1,\ldots,B_n \geqslant 1$ be given. Define \begin{align*} B = \max_{(e_1,\ldots,e_n)}\Big( \prod_{i\leqslant n} B_i^{e_i} \Big) \end{align*} where the maximum is taken over all integer $n$-tuples $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ for which the corresponding monomial $x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ occurs in $F$ with non-zero coefficient. Then there exists $D = D(n,d,\varepsilon)$ and an integer $k$ with \begin{align*} k \ll_{n,d,\varepsilon} T^\varepsilon (\log \|F\|)^{2n-3} \exp\Big((n-1)\Big(\frac{\prod_{i\leqslant n}\log B_i}{\log B}\Big)^{1/(n-1)}\Big) \end{align*} satisfying the following: There are $k$ polynomials $F_1,\ldots,F_k\in \mathbb{Z}[x_1 ,\ldots, x_n]$ coprime to $F$, with $\deg F_i \leqslant D$, such that every root of $F(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n)=0$ with $x_i \leqslant B_i$ is also a root of $F_j(x_1 ,\ldots, x_n)=0$, for some $j\leqslant k$.
nodes.label: thm:HeathBrownpadicDet

nodes.statement: Given integers $n,a_1,a_2\neq0$, there are at most $O_{\varepsilon,D}(|na_1a_2 X_1 X_2|^{\varepsilon})$ many solutions $(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ such that $|x_i|\leqslant X_i$ and \begin{align*} n = a_1 x_1^2 + a_2 x_2^2. \end{align*}
nodes.label: thm:QuadraticFormsEstimate

nodes.statement: Suppose $n=a_1x_1^2+a_2x_2^2$. Then $a_1n=a_1^2x_1^2+a_1a_2x_2^2$. Let $D$ be the squarefree part of $a_1a_2$. Then the number of solutions $(x_1,x_2)$ with $|x_i|\leqslant X_i$ to this equations is at most the number of solutions $(m_1,m_2)$ to $a_1n=m_1^2+Dm_2^2$ with $|m_i|\leqslant X_ia_1a_2$. For any such solution, we have $m_1+\sqrt{-D}m_2\mid a_1n$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D})$. The claim follows from the divisor bound in quadratic fields, in Lemma \ref{lem:DivisorBoundQuadField}.

Let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $D\geqslant1$ be a squarefree integer, and set $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-D})$. Then for all $\alpha\in K$, the number of ideals dividing $(\alpha)$ in $K$ is $O(N_\alpha^\varepsilon)$.

nodes.statement: Suppose now that $p=q\geqslant 2$. For $p=2$ this is a classical problem in quadratic forms. The bound $O_{\varepsilon,D}((|a_1a_2N|XY)^\varepsilon)$ follows from Heath-Brown~\cite[Theorem~3]{cubic}, for example.
